lessonTitle: Multifactorial and Mitochondrial Inheritance: Liability, Maternal Transmission and Heteroplasmy

blocks.text: A woman in her thirties has only mild exercise-induced muscle fatigue, yet her two children have very different illnesses: her son is healthy, while her daughter has seizures, stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis. The same maternal mutation, a different outcome. Mitochondria explain why, and a second family of diseases (such as type 2 diabetes) shows that genes alone rarely tell the whole story.

blocks.markdown: Many diseases do not follow Mendelian ratios. This lesson covers two non-Mendelian patterns: **multifactorial (complex) inheritance**, where many genes and environmental factors combine, and **mitochondrial inheritance**, where genes carried on the mitochondrial genome are transmitted through the egg cytoplasm.

blocks.title: Multifactorial inheritance
blocks.text: A trait or disease is multifactorial when it results from the combined effect of variants in several or many genes (each with a small effect, often called polygenic) together with environmental factors. There is no single causative mutation and no Mendelian ratio in families.

blocks.markdown: **The liability-threshold model.** Imagine that each person has an underlying *liability* to a disease, determined by all of their genetic and environmental risk factors added together. In the population, liability is roughly bell-shaped (normally distributed). Disease occurs only when liability exceeds a **threshold**. Relatives of an affected person share more risk alleles, so their liability curve is shifted toward the threshold and a larger area lies beyond it. Examples: cleft lip with or without cleft palate, congenital pyloric stenosis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease and many cancers. Environmental contributions (diet, smoking, intrauterine exposures) are essential; for instance identical (monozygotic) twins share all genes but are not always both affected, so concordance is well below 100%.

rows: Many variants of small effect plus environment
One gene, usually a single large-effect mutation
Recognisable dominant, recessive or X-linked pattern
Empirical, a few percent for first-degree relatives; falls rapidly for more distant relatives
Higher risk if the affected relative has severe disease or if more relatives are affected
Cleft lip, pyloric stenosis, type 2 diabetes
blocks.caption: Multifactorial versus Mendelian inheritance.

blocks.title: Rules of thumb for recurrence risk in multifactorial disease
blocks.text: Risk is highest for first-degree relatives, falls steeply for second- and third-degree relatives, increases with the number of affected relatives, increases with severity of the index case, and is higher when the index case is of the less commonly affected sex (the Carter effect), because that person must have carried a heavier load of risk factors. Recurrence risks are empirical figures measured in populations, not calculated from allele ratios.

blocks.title: Reading the threshold model for a sex-biased disease
blocks.prompt: Congenital pyloric stenosis affects about five times as many boys as girls. Using the liability-threshold model, explain why a son of an affected woman has a higher risk than a son of an affected man.

steps.text: Boys have a lower threshold (they develop disease with a smaller load of risk factors); girls have a higher threshold.
An affected woman has crossed the higher threshold, so she must carry a particularly large load of risk alleles.

She transmits half of her alleles to each child, so her children's mean liability is shifted further toward the threshold than the children of an affected man, who needed fewer risk factors to be affected.
A son, who has the lower threshold, is therefore at greatest risk when his mother is the affected parent.

blocks.answer: Because an affected female has crossed the higher threshold, she carries more risk alleles; her sons (with the lower threshold) have the highest recurrence risk.

blocks.markdown: **Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).** Each cell holds hundreds to thousands of mitochondria, each with several copies of a small circular genome (about 16.6 kilobases) encoding 37 genes: 13 polypeptide subunits of the respiratory chain and oxidative phosphorylation, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs. Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear genes, so mitochondrial disease may also be Mendelian. The mtDNA is inherited from the **mother only**: the oocyte contributes nearly all of the cytoplasm of the zygote, while mitochondria of the sperm are not passed on (they are largely eliminated). Therefore, a woman who carries a pathogenic mtDNA variant may transmit it to all her children (sons and daughters), whereas an affected man transmits it to none of his children. The pedigree shows no male-to-offspring transmission.

blocks.title: Heteroplasmy and homoplasmy
blocks.text: Heteroplasmy is the presence of a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA within a cell or individual. Homoplasmy means all copies are the same (all normal or all mutant). The proportion of mutant mtDNA is the mutant load (or heteroplasmy level).

blocks.markdown: **Why severity varies.** (1) *Threshold effect:* a cell tolerates a mixture of mutant and normal mtDNA until the mutant fraction exceeds a tissue-specific threshold (frequently high, of the order of 60-90% for many mutations), after which oxidative phosphorylation fails and symptoms appear. Tissues with high energy demand (brain, skeletal muscle, heart, retina, kidney) fail first. (2) *The germline bottleneck:* during oogenesis only a small number of mtDNA copies populate each developing oocyte, so the mutant load can differ greatly between siblings born to the same mother. (3) *Replicative (mitotic) segregation:* the mutant fraction drifts randomly in each cell lineage during development, giving different loads in different tissues. This explains why one mutation can cause very different disease severity in siblings, and why a mildly affected mother can have a severely affected child. Examples of mtDNA disease: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes), MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres) and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.

blocks.title: Interpreting a mutant load
blocks.prompt: A muscle biopsy from a patient yields 1800 sequence reads of a mitochondrial gene, of which 1350 carry the pathogenic variant. If the tissue threshold for symptoms is about 80% mutant, is this sample above threshold, and what does the result say about the mutant load in her ova?

steps.text: Mutant load equals mutant reads divided by total reads.
75% is below the assumed 80% threshold, so oxidative phosphorylation might be only partly compromised and her symptoms would be mild or modest.

Because of the germline bottleneck, the load in individual oocytes is not predictable from muscle: some ova may carry a much higher or lower load, so her children's severity cannot be predicted from 75%.

blocks.answer: The load is 75%, just below the assumed threshold (mild disease); the load in her ova and thus in her children's tissues is unpredictable because of the bottleneck.

items: Multifactorial: many genes plus environment; liability-threshold model; empirical recurrence risks.
Carter effect: more risk to relatives when the index case is of the less commonly affected sex.
Mitochondrial: maternal transmission only; affected fathers do not transmit.
Heteroplasmy: mixed normal and mutant mtDNA; severity depends on load, tissue threshold and the bottleneck.

blocks.title: Reading a pedigree
blocks.text: If a pedigree shows disease passed from affected mothers to all children of both sexes but never from affected fathers, think mitochondrial inheritance. Do not confuse it with X-linked inheritance, in which fathers do transmit to daughters.

points: Multifactorial disease results from many genes plus environment, modelled by liability beyond a threshold; recurrence risk is empirical and falls with distance of relationship.
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother, so an affected mother may pass it to all offspring while an affected father passes it to none.
Heteroplasmy, tissue thresholds and the oocyte bottleneck explain variable severity within a family.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is best described as multifactorial?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Cystic fibrosis
Huntington disease
Haemophilia A

distractorRationale.a: Correct: many genes and environmental factors (diet, obesity, activity) contribute.
distractorRationale.c: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant (CAG repeat in HTT).
distractorRationale.d: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive (factor VIII).

questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes arises from the combination of multiple susceptibility variants and environmental influences such as obesity. The other options are monogenic conditions with recognisable Mendelian patterns.

questions.stem: A man with a pathogenic mitochondrial DNA mutation has three children with a woman who has normal mtDNA. What is the expected inheritance of the mutation?

options.text: None of the children will inherit the mutation
All daughters but no sons will inherit it
All sons but no daughters will inherit it
Half of the children will inherit it

questions.correctOptionText: None of the children will inherit the mutation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: mtDNA is transmitted through the egg cytoplasm; sperm mitochondria are not passed on.
distractorRationale.b: This describes X-linked transmission, not mitochondrial.
distractorRationale.d: A 50% risk applies to autosomal dominant inheritance, not mtDNA.

questions.explanation: The zygote's mitochondria come from the oocyte cytoplasm, so mtDNA is inherited only from the mother. A man cannot transmit his mtDNA mutation to any of his children.

questions.stem: A mother has mild disease from a heteroplasmic mitochondrial mutation. Her first child is healthy, but her second child has severe disease. Which best explains the difference between the siblings?

options.text: A germline mtDNA bottleneck gives each oocyte a different mutant load
The second child inherited a paternal mtDNA copy that modified the mutation
Mitochondrial mutations follow autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance by sex
The mutation arose independently in the second child's nuclear genome

questions.correctOptionText: A germline mtDNA bottleneck gives each oocyte a different mutant load

distractorRationale.a: Correct: random sampling of mtDNA into each oocyte yields varying mutant loads between siblings.
distractorRationale.b: Paternal mtDNA is not transmitted to the offspring.
distractorRationale.c: mtDNA is not inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
distractorRationale.d: The mutation is in mtDNA, not nuclear DNA.

questions.explanation: During oogenesis only a few mtDNA molecules populate each oocyte, so the proportion of mutant mtDNA varies between eggs. Siblings may therefore have very different mutant loads and severity.

questions.stem: A family has several children with isolated cleft lip. Which statement about the recurrence risk for further siblings is most consistent with multifactorial inheritance?

options.text: The risk is higher than for a family with only one affected child, and is an empirical figure rather than 25% or 50%
The risk is exactly 25% for each subsequent pregnancy
The risk is exactly 50% for each subsequent pregnancy
The risk is unaffected by the number of affected relatives

questions.correctOptionText: The risk is higher than for a family with only one affected child, and is an empirical figure rather than 25% or 50%

distractorRationale.a: Correct: more affected relatives indicate a greater risk-factor load; the risk is empirical.
distractorRationale.b: 25% is the autosomal recessive risk; multifactorial risks are not fixed Mendelian fractions.
distractorRationale.c: 50% is the autosomal dominant risk, not applicable here.
distractorRationale.d: In multifactorial disease risk increases with the number of affected relatives.

questions.explanation: In multifactorial disease risks are empirical and increase when more close relatives are affected, since the family carries a heavier load of risk factors. Fixed Mendelian fractions do not apply.

questions.stem: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a multifactorial condition that is several times more common in girls than in boys. Which index patient's first-degree relatives are expected to have the highest recurrence risk, assuming equally severe disease?

options.text: An affected boy, because he belongs to the less commonly affected sex and so carried a high risk-factor load
An affected girl, because the condition is more frequent in her sex
Both are the same, because the sex of the index patient never alters risk
Neither, because multifactorial disease has no familial recurrence risk

questions.correctOptionText: An affected boy, because he belongs to the less commonly affected sex and so carried a high risk-factor load

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the Carter effect; the sex with the higher threshold (here boys) needs a heavier load of risk alleles to be affected.
distractorRationale.b: Girls have the lower threshold, so an affected girl does not necessarily carry an unusually large load.
distractorRationale.c: In multifactorial inheritance the sex of the index case does alter relatives' risk.
distractorRationale.d: Multifactorial disease does show familial clustering and raised recurrence risk.

questions.explanation: Boys have the higher liability threshold for this condition, so an affected boy must have a particularly heavy load of risk factors. His relatives share part of that load, so their recurrence risk is higher than for relatives of an affected girl.

questions.stem: Sequencing of a patient's blood mtDNA gives 2500 reads of a tRNA gene, of which 1000 carry a pathogenic variant. What is the percentage heteroplasmy (mutant load)? Give your answer in percent (%).
questions.explanation: Heteroplasmy is the fraction of mtDNA copies that carry the mutation: 1000 / 2500 = 0.40, which is 40%. Whether this load causes disease depends on the tissue threshold, which for many mutations is considerably higher.

questions.stem: True or false: Monozygotic twins who share 100% of their nuclear genes must both develop a multifactorial disease if one of them does.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Concordance for multifactorial disease in identical twins is well below 100% because environmental factors also contribute. Concordance well above that of non-identical twins, but below 100%, indicates both genetic and environmental influences.

questions.stem: Explain the liability-threshold model of multifactorial disease and use it to explain why the recurrence risk is higher for first-degree relatives than for third-degree relatives and higher when the affected relative has severe disease.
markingGuide: Liability is the combined effect of genetic and environmental risk factors, distributed approximately normally in the population.
Disease occurs when liability exceeds a threshold.
Relatives share genes with the index case in proportion to relatedness, shifting their liability distribution towards the threshold.
First-degree relatives share about half of their alleles; third-degree relatives share much less, so risk falls rapidly with distance.
Severe disease indicates a high liability (large load of risk alleles), so relatives are shifted further toward the threshold.
Environmental factors also contribute, so risk is not 100% even in identical twins.
questions.explanation: In the model, the closer the relative, the more risk alleles shared and the greater the shift in liability. Severe disease suggests a heavy genetic load, increasing the risk further.

questions.stem: Describe the pattern of mitochondrial inheritance as it would appear in a pedigree, and explain the biological basis for this pattern.
markingGuide: Transmission is only through the mother; affected mothers can pass to sons and daughters.
Affected fathers do not transmit to any offspring.
Zygote cytoplasm and mitochondria derive from the oocyte; sperm mitochondria are not passed on.
mtDNA is a small circular genome with 37 genes (13 proteins, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs).
Severity varies between affected relatives because of heteroplasmy.
questions.explanation: Because mitochondria come with the egg's cytoplasm, mtDNA mutations are passed only along the maternal line to children of both sexes. Variable severity reflects heteroplasmy.

questions.stem: Define heteroplasmy. Explain three reasons why the severity of mitochondrial disease can differ between two siblings who share the same maternal mutation, and why organs such as brain and skeletal muscle are often affected first.
markingGuide: Heteroplasmy is the coexistence of mutant and normal mtDNA in the same cell or individual.
Threshold effect: disease appears only when mutant load exceeds a tissue-specific threshold.
Germline bottleneck: oocytes receive a random sample of mtDNA, so mutant load differs between siblings.
Replicative (mitotic) segregation: random drift of mutant load in different tissues and cell lineages during development.
High-energy-demand tissues (brain, skeletal muscle, heart, retina) depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation and so are affected at lower mutant loads.
questions.explanation: A mixture of mutant and normal mtDNA means the effect depends on the proportion present. Random sampling at the bottleneck and during development gives different loads, and organs with high ATP demand exceed their threshold first.
